COMMENT OF GREEN
RECURSIVE UTILITY SERVICE
LLC

Before the Public Utility Commission
of Texas

Project No. 58317 — Registration and
Reporting of Large Computational Loads


(Companion filing to Carriage Tariff GRUS-
FERC-2026-001, FERC CID C013240)

Filed by: Green Recursive Utility Service LLC (GRUS
LLC)
Texas SOS 806584578 · PUCT Control No. 59976 ·
FERC CID C013240 · SAM UEI [on file]
205 East 3rd Street, Weatherford, Texas 76086
management@greenrecursiveutilityservice.org ·
817-404-6379
Date: July 2026
 I. INTEREST OF THE COMMENTER
AND SUMMARY

Green Recursive Utility Service LLC is a Texas data-
infrastructure utility operating under a carriage tariff
of record before this Commission (Control No. 59976,
Item 1) and the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (CID C013240).

GRUS submits this comment because Project No.
58317 confronts a problem this Commission cannot
fully solve with the tools presently before it, and GRUS
holds the missing tool.

The problem: the Commission is asked to bring large
computational loads — data centers — under a
registration and reporting framework so that ERCOT
can forecast and manage them. But a computational
load is presently a black box. The Commission can
meter the megawatts a facility draws at its
interconnection point. It cannot meter what
determines that draw — the efficiency of the
computation inside the facility. The 438 GW in the
ERCOT large-load queue is 438 GW of black boxes
whose internal consumption is unmeasured and
unregulated.

The missing tool: a standard unit and a standard
meter for computational load itself. Until a load can
be measured in a standard unit, it cannot be regulated
 — only observed at its boundary. This is the same
condition electricity was in before the kilowatt-hour:
consumable, but not regulable, because there was no
standard unit and no meter.

What GRUS offers: a defined, patented two-layer
standard that supplies both the unit and the meter for
computational load, and a utility service, already
tariffed, that reduces that load — delivering grid relief
at the point where the load is created rather than at
the point where it is drawn.

GRUS does not ask the Commission to adopt GRUS's
commercial tariff. GRUS offers its measurement
standard as the basis on which the Commission may
finally meter what it seeks to regulate, and identifies
itself as a registered federal and state entity prepared
to provide that capability.




II. THE REGULATORY GAP: A GRID
WITHOUT A METER

A. Computational load is a grid of the same
structural class as the electrical grid

A regulable grid, in structural terms, is a metered
network of interconnected nodes across which a
measurable physical quantity flows and can be
 accounted at each node. The electrical grid is the
familiar instance.

Data infrastructure is another instance of the same
class. Within and across data centers, electrical
charge is gated across interconnected computational
nodes — transistors, boards, racks, facilities — in
precisely the manner charge is switched across the
interconnected nodes of the electrical grid,
distinguished by scale and frequency rather than by
kind. A populated computing board, examined at its
own scale, is a distribution network: power planes as
feeders, conductive traces as lines, switching
elements as loads.

This is not a metaphor offered for color. It is the
physical basis on which the Commission's jurisdiction
can reach the problem. The computational load and
the electrical load are not two separate phenomena
that happen to correlate. They are one continuous
system of gated charge, observed at two scales. The
heat a data center rejects and the water it consumes
to reject that heat are the downstream physical
consequences of the switching activity within it.
Reduce the switching, and the megawatts, the heat,
and the water all fall together, because they are the
same physical event measured at different points.


B. Why this grid has never been regulated
 The electronics industry reached grid scale within
approximately the last twenty years. Regulatory layers
do not attach to a new industry at its inception; they
attach when the aggregate quantity becomes large
enough to strain shared infrastructure and when a
standard unit of measurement makes the quantity
accountable. Structural steel had no load ratings or
building codes for decades after its introduction; the
regulatory layer arrived only once standardized grades
and standardized measurement made the material
accountable.

Computational load has now reached the scale — 438
GW in the ERCOT queue, nearly 90% from data centers
— at which it strains shared infrastructure. What it has
lacked, and what has prevented its regulation, is a
standard unit and a meter. That is the gap this
comment addresses.




III. THE STANDARD: A TWO-LAYER
METER FOR COMPUTATIONAL LOAD

GRUS holds two United States patent applications
that together define a complete, closed, measurable
standard for computational load. They were filed to
operate as one system, and each defines a layer the
other requires.
 A. The format layer — the unit (USPTO
19/700,381, Compressed Memory Manifold)

The Compressed Memory Manifold defines a
standard representation of data in a fixed, hardware-
aligned form — delimiter-free, map-free, addressed by
computed offset against a 64-byte hardware
boundary. This is the unit of measurement. Data
represented in this form has a defined, measurable
consumption profile: a fixed relationship between the
work performed and the memory transactions, cache
behavior, CPU cycles, energy, and heat it produces.

Because the format is fixed and hardware-aligned, its
resource consumption is determinable rather than
estimated. This is what makes it a meter. Just as the
kilowatt-hour is a defined unit that makes electrical
consumption accountable, the CMM-formatted
representation is a defined unit that makes
computational consumption accountable.


B. The substrate layer — the operation (USPTO
19/710,080, Intelligent Intelligence Class II)

Intelligent Intelligence Class II defines the computing
substrate that operates on the CMM-formatted
representation. Its specification names CMM as its
storage substrate; the two are bound by the patent
record itself, not by assertion. II-II defines the
operation that consumes the metered format — the
 anchored, deterministic computation that runs on the
grid the format defines.


C. Why both layers are required to close the
meter

The two layers together define a closed system, and
neither alone is sufficient:

    The format layer alone defines a unit but not the
    operation that consumes it.

    The substrate layer alone defines an operation but
    not the measurable unit it is accounted in.

Together they define both what flows across the
computational grid — CMM-formatted load — and
what operates on it — the II-II substrate. Load that is
represented in the format and processed on the
substrate is measurable, at each node, in a standard
unit. That is a closed, meterable grid.


D. The scope boundary — drawn exactly on the
standard

The regulable object defined by this standard is
computational load consumed through the CMM-
formatted, II-II-operated substrate. The boundary is
the standard itself.

This boundary is deliberately precise, and its precision
is what makes it defensible and non-overreaching:
    Load that consumes the CMM-formatted
   substrate is measurable in the defined unit and is
   within scope.

   Computation that does not use the standard —
   that runs on conventional, unaligned, delimiter-
   bearing representations — is not measured by this
   meter and is outside this instrument. Such
   computation forgoes the substrate's efficiency
   and reverts to conventional consumption; whether
   the Commission regulates that separately is a
   matter for the Commission, on subject matter this
   standard does not reach.

The meter measures what the standard defines. It
claims nothing beyond the standard.




IV. THE TRANSPORT-LAYER SCOPE:
A CLEAN, EXISTING REGULATORY
LINE

The standard applies at the transport layer — the point
at which computational demand crosses the
interconnected data-infrastructure grid — and not to
passive or isolated endpoints. This boundary is not
novel; it is the boundary communications and utility
regulation already draws.
     A passive endpoint receiving an already-regulated
    signal — a radio receiver, a television — transports
    no load onto the data-infrastructure grid and is
    outside scope. Its transport layer, where one
    exists, is already regulated as spectrum.

    A device performing isolated local computation
    for itself, not interconnected to shared data
    infrastructure, transports no load onto the grid
    and is outside scope.

    A request that places computational demand onto
    interconnected shared data infrastructure — a
    query to a data center, a cloud inference call, a
    compute job dispatched to a remote hub — is a
    transported load, crosses the transport layer, and
    is within scope.

The regulated object is the transported load at the
interconnection, exactly as communications law
regulates the transport layer rather than the
endpoint's private activity. This yields a binary,
physically observable test: did computational demand
cross the interconnected transport layer, or did it
not? The meter sits at that boundary, which is also the
boundary of regulable interest, which is also the
boundary of the CMM-formatted standard. The unit
measured, the layer regulated, and the point charged
are the same physical event.
 V. THE SERVICE: GRID RELIEF AT
THE POINT OF LOAD CREATION

The measurement standard is the instrument; the
utility service is its application.

GRUS's audited reference measurement documents,
against a conventional baseline, reductions of the
physical quantities that constitute grid strain: memory
transactions −91.2%, CPU cycles −97.5%, peak power
−82.4%, storage −64.3%, with cache miss rates falling
from 40.2% to 0.81%. These are instrumented
measurements of physical reduction, not projections.

Applied at data-center scale, this is demand-side grid
relief acting at the point where the load is created —
inside the computation — rather than at the point
where it is drawn from the grid. This is a category the
Commission already possesses authority over and
mechanisms to fund: load management and
efficiency. What is new is that the reduction is
achieved within the computation itself, through a
metered standard, rather than by throttling or
curtailing the facility.

A data center consuming through the CMM-formatted
substrate places materially less load on the ERCOT
grid for the same work. Metered against the standard,
that reduction is measurable, verifiable, and
attributable — which is precisely what a registration-
 and-reporting framework under Project No. 58317
requires and presently lacks.




VI. WHAT GRUS PROPOSES TO THE
COMMISSION

GRUS respectfully submits the following for the
Commission's consideration in this rulemaking:

 1. That the Commission recognize the absence of a
   standard unit and meter for computational load
   as the operative gap in bringing large
   computational loads under an effective
   registration-and-reporting framework.

 2. That GRUS's two-layer standard — the CMM
   format as the unit and the II-II substrate as the
   operation — be considered as a basis for
   metering computational load in a standard,
   verifiable unit at the transport-layer boundary.

 3. That the engineering specification of the
   metering methodology, which GRUS is preparing
   for filing as a formal standard suitable for
   regulatory adoption and independent verification,
   be received into the record of this or a successor
   proceeding.
  4. That GRUS be recognized as a registered federal
    and state data-infrastructure utility — of record
    before this Commission (59976), FERC (CID
    C013240), and SAM.gov — prepared to provide
    computational-load metering and demand-side
    grid relief as a utility service.

GRUS does not ask the Commission to adopt GRUS's
commercial rate. GRUS offers the measurement
standard the Commission needs to regulate what it
presently can only observe, and identifies itself as the
entity prepared to provide it.




VII. CONCLUSION

The Commission is asked in this proceeding to bring
an unmetered grid under regulation. That cannot be
done by measuring the load only at its boundary; it
requires a standard unit and a meter for the load
itself. The data-infrastructure grid is real, it is of the
same structural class as the electrical grid, it has
reached the scale at which it strains shared
infrastructure, and it has lacked only the unit and the
meter that make regulation possible.

GRUS holds that unit and that meter, defined in two
patents built to operate as one system, bounded
precisely to what the standard defines, applied at the
transport layer where existing law already draws the
 regulable line. GRUS offers them to the Commission
as the basis on which Texas may finally regulate the
data-infrastructure grid — and reduce the load it
places on the electrical grid — in a standard every
consumer can be held to uniformly.

Respectfully submitted,

Nicholas Wray Cordova
Principal and Inventor of Record
Green Recursive Utility Service LLC — Weatherford,
Texas
